topic: Economic Objectives and the Role of Government
subject: economics

items.title: The Soviet economy grew faster than the US for decades
items.claim: From the 1928 first Five-Year Plan to the late 1960s, how did Soviet growth compare to US growth?

options.text: The Soviet economy was always smaller and grew more slowly than the US
Soviet GDP growth averaged roughly 5-6% annually through the 1950s, faster than the US in the same period — before stagnating sharply in the 1970s-80s
Soviet GDP collapsed in 1932 and never recovered
The Soviet economy never produced reliable statistics

items.reveal:
CIA estimates put Soviet GDP growth at 5.7% (1950s) and 5.2% (1960s), against US rates of 3-4%. The growth was 'extensive' — pulling labour out of agriculture, building heavy industry, exploiting massive natural resources — rather than 'intensive' productivity gains.

By the 1970s the extensive sources were exhausted. Innovation faltered, oil propped up the system in the 1970s, then the 1980s collapse came when oil prices fell and reform under Gorbachev destabilised what remained.

Robert Allen, Stephen Kotkin and others have documented this trajectory in detail.
items.why: 'Communism never works' as a one-liner ignores 40 years of measurable, fast growth. The interesting question is why the model worked for extensive industrialisation but failed at the next stage.

items.title: Perfect competition is a benchmark, not a description
items.claim: Perfect competition (many small firms, homogeneous products, free entry, perfect information) is taught as a foundational market structure. Which is most accurate?

options.text: Most real markets fit the model closely
Real-world markets rarely satisfy the assumptions; agriculture, currency trading and some commodity markets come closer than most. The model is useful as a normative benchmark, not as descriptive
Perfect competition is identical to monopoly
No real-world market resembles it at all

items.reveal:
Monopolistic competition (Chamberlin 1933) and game-theoretic oligopoly models (Cournot 1838, Bertrand 1883, Stackelberg 1934) capture more of the realistic market structures.

Key deviations: most product markets have differentiated products; information is imperfect (Akerlof's 'lemons' 1970); entry has costs; small numbers of dominant firms common. The 'IO revolution' from the 1970s onwards (Tirole's textbook, 1988) built strategic-interaction-based frameworks.
items.why: The perfect competition model serves as a welfare benchmark in policy analysis. Treating it as a description of how markets work misses what most of industrial economics has been building toward.

items.title: US tariffs on China were largely absorbed by US importers
items.claim: Amiti, Redding and Weinstein (Journal of Economic Perspectives, 2019) studied the incidence of 2018 US tariffs on Chinese imports. What did they find?

options.text: Chinese exporters paid the entire tariff
Nearly the full cost of the tariffs was passed through to US importers and consumers; producer prices in China barely changed. The 'tariffs hurt foreigners' framing did not match the price data

items.reveal:
Amiti, Redding and Weinstein analysed customs and price data through 2019. The pass-through was nearly complete to US importers; Chinese export prices for affected goods didn't drop substantially.

Fajgelbaum, Goldberg, Kennedy and Khandelwal (QJE 2020) confirmed the finding using different methods. Subsequent Biden-era tariffs (2024) followed similar patterns. The US-China tariffs reshaped supply chains (Vietnam, Mexico saw substantial increases in exports to the US) more than they raised significant revenue.
items.why: The political rhetoric of tariffs often diverges from the economic incidence. Trade policy effects are empirically measurable; the empirics often don't support the political framing.
